common_name: Amy Chinese Chestnut (Extremely Cold-Hardy Ohio-Bred Selection)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Amy needs a second, genetically distinct Chinese chestnut cultivar such as Qing, Gideon, or Peach planted nearby for reliable cross-pollination.

directions: Amy is a Greg Miller selection (numbered 72-400) chosen from a 1972 planting of Chinese chestnut seedlings grown from Ackerman Nursery stock in Carrollton, Ohio, the same planting that produced the Gideon and Peach cultivars. It stands out for exceptional cold hardiness, reliably surviving winters at least to USDA zone 5b, well beyond the comfort range of many Chinese chestnut selections, while still budding out early and cropping heavily and consistently once established. Nuts are small to medium and shrink somewhat further as the tree matures, but carry excellent flavor and peel cleanly, and like other Chinese chestnuts Amy carries the species' natural resistance to chestnut blight that eliminated American chestnut from eastern forests. Because chestnuts are self-incompatible, plant a second unrelated Chinese chestnut cultivar within pollination range for a full nut set, and site trees in deep, well-drained soil since Amy can be prone to blossom-end nut disorders in poorly drained ground.
sources: University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry — Descriptions of Chestnut Cultivars for Nut Production (HortScience, 2021)

common_name: Jenny Chinese Chestnut (Tall Early-Ripening Kintzel-Derived Selection)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, allowing extra room for Jenny's tall, erect habit; a second, genetically distinct Chinese chestnut cultivar is needed nearby for pollination.

directions: Jenny was selected by chestnut breeder J.M. Nave as an open-pollinated seedling of the old West Virginia cultivar Kintzel, and has since been evaluated in Missouri chestnut trials. Unlike the broad, spreading orchard-type crown typical of many Chinese chestnut selections, Jenny grows as a tall, vigorous, erect tree with unusually large leaves, so it benefits from extra vertical space. It ripens early and drops its large, exceptionally flavorful nuts within a short window once the first ones fall, which simplifies harvest compared with cultivars that drop nuts over many weeks. Inheriting the blight resistance and cold hardiness of its Kintzel parent along with the natural resistance of Chinese chestnut generally, Jenny is only rarely troubled by chestnut blight. Because chestnuts will not self-pollinate, plant a second, unrelated Chinese chestnut cultivar within range for a reliable nut set.
sources: University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry — Descriptions of Chestnut Cultivars for Nut Production (HortScience, 2021)

common_name: Marsol Chestnut (Vigorous French Hybrid, Ink Disease and Rust Tolerant)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees while dormant in late winter in deep, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun; Marsol benefits from a compatible hybrid chestnut cultivar such as Marigoule or Bouche de Betizac nearby for pollination.

directions: Marsol, also recorded as Maraval 07, is an open-pollinated selection from France's INRA chestnut breeding program at Lalevade-d'Ardeche, part of the same European x Japanese hybrid family that produced Marigoule, Maridonne, and Precoce Migoule. It is prized above all for its vigor and outstanding graft compatibility, which has made it a leading rootstock choice, more vigorous than the related Maraval and on par with Bouche de Betizac and Comballe, but it also bears attractive, large reddish nuts, averaging roughly 26 grams each, with good flavor and easy peeling. As a sativa x crenata hybrid, Marsol carries meaningful resistance to chestnut blight and chestnut rust, and its roots show some tolerance of ink disease (Phytophthora), a soil-borne pathogen that has damaged pure European chestnut plantings. Chestnuts are self-incompatible, so plant a second, genetically distinct hybrid chestnut cultivar nearby for a full nut set.
sources: INRA (French National Institute for Agricultural Research) — chestnut breeding program records
University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry — chestnut cultivar trials
